template.title: Execution
template.subtitle: Build the first version
template.intro: You run the build in the goal tracker. The program points say what result is required. Extra goals don't block moving on.
general.title: General
general.intro: These points apply to every build. The categories add their own results.
general/next.title: Choose the nearest result and assign the work
general/next.guide_body:
1.1. Decide what should be ready
Start with the work whose result will let you take the next step in the build. Draw on the earlier findings and the requirements of your category. If you already have a suitable Goal, that is a saved goal, open its card. Fill in only the missing information.
Name the goal so that, once it's done, you can check what was created. Just “Work on the product” says little. A helpful pattern is: “A finished [part] that lets you [do a specific action]”. If several independent results hide under one name, choose the one needed soonest or split the work into smaller goals.
Already now, decide on the proof, that is the evidence of completion. It can be a specific file, a photo, a recording of it working or a record of a test result. Match it to the goal and the requirements of the program point. A photo can show what an object looks like, but confirming that it works may need a recording or a test result. At the start you define what you'll show; you add the actual proof after the work is done.
1.2. Assign the work and set a deadline
Choose one person who will see the whole goal through. They can use other people's help, but they're responsible for gathering the necessary parts and seeing the work to the end. Use the division of responsibility set in Preparation. When you work alone, you're the owner of the goal.
Agree on the deadline with the person doing the work. Take into account their availability and whether they first need the result of someone else's work. If the whole thing is too big for the chosen deadline, carve out a smaller result that can be achieved in that time. Keep the remaining work for later.
Add tasks when they help split the work between people or set its order. Each should clearly say what needs to be done. Avoid breaking things down into individual clicks and obvious actions. If someone is waiting for another person's result, agree on a date for handing over that part.
Attach the materials without which the person doing the work would have to look for information or keep asking. Choose the current document or a file already saved in Vairo. Materials about other work can stay where they are.
general/next.guide_sources.0: Geoff Ralston, YC’s Essential Startup Advice (2017): focusing on the most important work and simplifying the scope. The description of Goals and proof is an adaptation for Vairo.
general/next.guide_sources.1: Y Combinator, 10 Questions to Discuss with a Potential Co-founder (2023): dividing responsibility, availability and setting the order of work. Assignments in Goal and task cards apply these guidelines in Vairo.
general/next/setup.title: Set the result, owner, deadline and proof
general/next/setup.description: The goal can still be in progress. Tasks and materials are optional.
general/next/setup/open.question: Open an existing goal or create one for the nearest work.
general/next/setup/open.help: A click alone doesn't complete the point. What counts is a goal with a named result, an owner, a deadline and an agreed proof.
general/next/setup/open.config.label: Create a goal from the Preparation list
general/work.title: Take the work through to a completed result
general/work.guide_body:
2.1. Record progress on the work you're doing
You can do the work in the tools chosen for it. Come back to the card in Vairo when the state of a task has changed, a useful result has been created or an obstacle has appeared. The update is meant to let you and the team quickly see what's ready and what needs doing next.
Record only the information needed for further work. Example: “The first variant is ready. [part] is still missing. Current file: [link]”. If a status change and an attached file are enough, end the update there. A separate report on the whole day isn't needed.
When you come back to the work, use the same card. A shared record avoids a situation in which one person works on an old version while another looks for the result in messages.
2.2. Unblock the work if you get stuck
Set the “Blocked” status when a specific obstacle makes further work impossible. Describe it so that it's clear what's missing. “I'm waiting for a decision on which of the two variants we prepare” gives the team more information than “I can't move”. Simply passing a deadline means a delay; it doesn't have to mean a blocker.
Decide on the nearest action that will remove the obstacle and assign it to a specific person. For example: “Ola will choose the variant by Thursday”. Record it in an existing task or add a task under the goal. When the help requires changing the person or the deadline, correct the existing assignment.
If the obstacle concerns the way of doing it, consider a simpler route to the same needed result. At the start, part of the work can be done by hand or with someone's help. Such a simplification must still meet the goal's requirements. Record the chosen solution with the work, so the other people know how to continue.
2.3. Close the achieved goal
Compare the result with what was meant to be created. If the goal hasn't been achieved yet, leave it open and fix the tasks. Ticking off all the activities isn't enough when their expected effect is missing.
Distinguish a goal of checking something from a goal of building a working part. If the goal was to run a test, its negative result is also a result to record. If the goal was to get a working part, a failed test means this goal needs more work. This way the team sees both the check that was done and the remaining problem.
When the goal has been achieved, point to the required proof and mark it as completed. You can use material already saved in the card. Make sure you're showing the right version and that the proof matches what was meant to be confirmed.
Vairo will take the result into account in the explicitly linked program points. The first completed Goal lets you complete this General point. You still do the remaining build requirements in your categories, using the same cards and working rules.
general/work.guide_sources.0: Michael Seibel, The Scientific Method for Startups (2016): making decisions based on observed results. The way of recording progress in work cards is an adaptation of this principle for Vairo.
general/work.guide_sources.1: Paul Graham, Do Things that Don’t Scale (2013): using simple, including manual, ways of working at the start. Handling obstacles and assigning actions follow from the way of working adopted in Vairo.
general/work.guide_sources.2: Michael Seibel, The Scientific Method for Startups (2016): testing assumptions, drawing conclusions and continuing work based on results. The rules for completing a Goal and completing points come from the Vairo program.
general/work/done.title: Close the achieved goal
general/work/done.description: One explicitly linked goal of the current build, completed and with the required proof.
general/work/done/open.question: Point to the proof and mark the goal as completed.
general/work/done/open.help: If there's no result yet, leave the goal open and fix the tasks.
general/work/done/open.config.label: Open goals
general/close.title: Close Execution
general/close.duration_hint: When the other requirements are met
general/close.guide_body:
3.1. Finish the required work
Open the stage summary and check the gaps shown. If the work is done but there's no saved proof, attach the existing result. If the result itself is missing, go back to the relevant Goal and finish the work. Use the requirements of General and the chosen categories.
Separate a gap needed to finish the first version from an idea for expanding it further. A helpful question: “Without this change, will the first version do what it's meant to provide for the user?”. Extras can stay in open Goals. The requirements on functioning and safety that come from your categories have to be met before moving on.
3.2. Move on to the MVP Stage
When the remaining requirements are met, the Founder or an Admin confirms the end of Execution. The summary uses the results recorded earlier. You don't need to prepare another description of all the work done.
In the MVP Stage you'll work on making the first version available to recipients, collecting their reactions and making further improvements. The tracker, the team, the materials and open Goals remain available. Finishing the build doesn't yet settle how recipients will use the product. That's why you'll also base further work on what happens after it's made available.
general/close.guide_sources.0: Geoff Ralston, YC’s Essential Startup Advice (2017): limiting unnecessary expansion of the first version. Paul Graham, Do Things that Don’t Scale (2013): avoiding putting off first use while waiting for perfection, taking the consequences of mistakes into account. The list of required work comes from the Vairo program.
general/close.guide_sources.1: Geoff Ralston, YC’s Essential Startup Advice (2017): releasing a useful first version and further improvements based on contact with users. The conditions for moving on to the MVP Stage and keeping the data follow from Vairo's rules.
general/close/summary.title: Check what's missing
general/close/summary.description: This point isn't a condition for the finish button to appear.
general/close/summary/open.question: Open the stage summary and fill in the missing results.
general/close/summary/open.help: The finish button counts the other required points, not this sub-point.
general/close/summary/open.config.label: Summary
saas.title: SaaS
saas.intro: The first version of the program: how it works, access, data, tests and readiness for improvements.
saas/saas-core.title: Build the program's main action
saas/saas-core.guide_body:
1.1. Take the user to the first result
Open the description of the first version prepared earlier. Choose the main action the program is to enable and take it to a working result. If you're building a tool for preparing reports, the user should be able to hand over data and get the right report. Already during the build, you can show this path on a simple example. This lets you notice early that individual parts of the program don't work together the way you assumed.
Link an existing Goal or create a Goal of the “Build result” type. It could read: “The user adds a data file and downloads a report prepared from it”. Assign a responsible person, agree on a deadline and name the expected proof, that is the evidence of completion. In this example it could be a recording of the whole action and the report received. Agreeing on the result before starting work makes it easier to check later whether the task was done.
Split the work where a specific piece can be handed over. One person can prepare accepting the file, another the calculations, and a third the result view. Agree beforehand on what data these parts pass to each other. The person responsible for the Goal also keeps an eye on how they connect. When someone says their part is ready, check it with the part that's meant to use it. In Vairo, tasks under a shared goal are enough. Size each task so its result can be shown and checked.
If you're using a ready-made platform for building apps without writing code, you can get the same result by configuring its features. When the recipient of the service is another program, the connection goes through an API, that is an agreed way of exchanging data between programs. In that case, show sending the necessary data and the response received. With longer processing, the recipient should be able to check whether the work is running, has finished or needs retrying.
Attach to the proof the result obtained on sample data and the label of the version tested. The version can have a simple name, e.g. “0.1”, linked to a code commit or the history of the ready-made platform. This way the team will know what the recording refers to after further changes are made. Use the same material in the next sub-points if it also answers their questions.
saas/saas-core.guide_sources.0: Google Engineering Practices, Small CLs describes working through small changes that can be reviewed separately. Atlassian, Roles and Responsibilities explains agreeing on the responsibility and involvement of collaborators. The example and the way of running a Goal have been adapted to Vairo.
saas/saas-core/result.title: Take the user to the first result
saas/saas-core/result/open.question: Link or create a goal of the “Build result” type.
saas/saas-core/result/open.help: The proof shows the version, the action and the result.
saas/saas-core/result/open.config.label: Open goals
saas/saas-access.title: Take care of access and data
saas/saas-access.guide_body:
2.1. Put the program's access rules in place
Use the findings from Preparation and pass them to the person building access. They should know who can enter the program and what actions are available to that person. For user accounts, it's worth using ready-made login mechanisms. Also check how a user regains access when they lose their password or the chosen login method stops working. In a public program, certain actions can be available without an account, while managing the service still needs protection.
Logging in confirms the user's identity. Permissions define what they're allowed to do with a specific material. The person who created a report may have the right to change it, while an invited recipient can only read it. If the program serves several companies, access to one of them shouldn't open the data of the others. Apply the same rule to the private accounts of individuals.
Prepare two test accounts with separate materials. Ask a technical person to check whether the second account can read or change someone else's material, including by sending a request directly to the service. A hidden button doesn't protect such a request. The check has to work in the part of the program that handles requests and serves data. With a ready-made platform, its access settings have to be checked in the configuration used.
If access is paid, put the rules chosen earlier in place. Confirmation of payment should come from a trustworthy source, e.g. the payment provider's system. When you unlock accounts by hand at first, agree on who checks the payment and for how long they grant access. The end of the paid period and cancelling the next renewal should lead to the behaviour set in Preparation.
Choose the person responsible for the technical check based on their skills. As the founder, you can set the rules and review the result together with them. In the proof, keep a description of the working access and the results of the tests on the test accounts. This material will come in handy again when checking the whole program in sub-point 3.1.
2.2. Handle data throughout the program
Follow one piece of information through the program. For example, the user adds a file to a project, the program creates a report, and the user opens it again later. Check that the report uses the right file and stays assigned to the right project. A few easily distinguishable pieces of test data are enough. They'll help you notice that two projects were mixed up or that the result wasn't kept after coming back.
Agree with the person doing the work on what data the program can accept. If it expects a number of orders, it should react appropriately to text or a disallowed value. If it accepts files, it needs to check their type and allowed size. The check should happen before processing on the service side. A message next to the form helps the user correct a mistake, but a check in the browser alone can be bypassed.
Pay attention to actions that change several things at once. When booking a place, the program may save the booking and reduce the number of free places. Agree on what happens if saving the booking succeeds and the second step is interrupted. Related changes in one database can often be combined into a transaction, that is an operation carried out in full or rolled back. When the work involves different services, the person doing it has to choose a way of recognizing the completed steps and safely finishing or undoing the rest.
Apply the agreed way of keeping and deleting information. A file and the link to it can be stored in different places. So removing an entry from the screen doesn't have to delete the file itself. Check what happens to the data in the places the program uses, also after access ends. If a result is only needed during a single processing run, make sure that processing ends and the data is deleted according to the agreed rules.
A shared Goal can cover the whole path of the data, even when different people prepare its pieces. Agree on the moment of a joint test, so you catch mistakes in passing information along. As proof, keep a description of the check and its result. Use the materials created during the work, without copying technical documentation into another form.
saas/saas-access.guide_sources.0: OWASP, Authorization Cheat Sheet explains permissions and access checks on the service side. AWS, Tenant isolation describes separating customers' resources. Stripe, Webhooks presents verifying the origin of notifications from the payment provider.
saas/saas-access.guide_sources.1: OWASP, Input Validation Cheat Sheet describes checking input data and files. PostgreSQL, Transactions explains the principle of committing related database changes together. The scope of keeping and deleting data follows from your product's findings.
saas/saas-access/rules.title: Put the program's access rules in place
saas/saas-access/rules/open.question: Show that the chosen way of access works.
saas/saas-access/rules/open.config.label: Open goals
saas/saas-access/data.title: Handle data throughout the program
saas/saas-access/data/open.question: Describe the working data handling and point to the result of checking it.
saas/saas-access/data/open.config.label: Open goals
saas/saas-check.title: Check the program while it's in use
saas/saas-check.guide_body:
3.1. Check the result of the action and the reaction to problems
Start the test from the situation a new recipient will be in. Prepare a fresh account or another way of getting in that suits the product. Do the main action without using the materials left on the creator's account. Also check the result itself. A report may open and at the same time contain wrong calculations. A program summarizing text may return an answer that leaves out the most important information.
Then check the behaviour on a mistake or interruption. What will the user see when they upload the wrong file? Will it be clear that an external service didn't respond? Where repeating an action could create a second booking or charge a fee again, also check retrying the same request. The effect of the operation should match the user's intention. Use the results of the access checks from sub-point 2.1 if they still apply to the version tested.
With connections to external services, you sometimes receive automatic messages about events. They're called webhooks. Such a message may be information that access has been paid for. The person doing the work should verify its origin using the method the provider specifies and handle repeated delivery. Also check delays and a different order of messages, if the integration can work that way. For payments, use the provider's test environment, so the tests don't charge any money.
Split the checks by skills. A person who knows the user's needs can judge whether the action is understandable and whether the report is correct. A technical person will check the requests sent to the service and its behaviour on errors. If you work alone, use the expectations written down earlier and suitable help for matters you can't judge. Repeatable checks of key operations are worth considering with the person doing the work as tests run automatically after changes.
With a Goal of the “Test result” type, keep the version tested and the results. A record that lets you reproduce the test is enough, e.g. “A file without a date was added. A message about the missing date was expected. The program created an empty report”. Such a result can complete a Goal about running a test. The problem found still needs fixing before the feature is confirmed as ready. The collected tests can stay in one document attached as proof.
3.2. Check the load and the cost of use
Go back to the number of first users and the way of use assumed in Preparation. Recreate the expected work on the prepared version of the program. If several people can create reports at the same time, check exactly that situation. Measure the waiting time and see whether all the jobs finish correctly. The number of accounts alone doesn't show the load. What matters is what users do at the same time and how large the data they process is.
Start with a small test and increase the load to the range needed. Agree with the person doing the work on a safe way to run it on your service. With connections to external providers, take into account their testing terms and available limits. State which configuration the test was run on. A result from a more powerful machine may not match how the program works on the cheaper plan you plan to offer recipients.
Look at the use of services during the actions performed. A month's cost can be roughly estimated as the fixed fees plus the cost of the expected use. For example, with a fixed fee of $12 and a cost of 5 cents per report, doing 50 reports would cost about $14.50 in total. This is only an example calculation. Use your providers' prices and include the program's other paid actions. A longer file or retrying a failed processing run can change the cost.
If the expected use exceeds the budget, limit what generates the spending. It may be the number of reports or the length of the uploaded recording. Check with the person doing the work that the limit also works for a direct request to the service. On reaching the limit, the user should get understandable information. If the chosen provider itself provides the needed limit, check how it works and what effect it has for the recipient.
Add the test conditions and the results obtained to the proof. Also write down the cost estimate for the first group and the limits needed. Separate measurement from prediction: “we did 20 reports” describes a test, while “100 reports will cost about…” describes a calculation. The person responsible for this Goal should agree the technical result with the person doing the work, and the acceptable cost with the person keeping an eye on the budget.
3.3. Fix the problem and check the change
Use this sub-point when you find a defect during the work. Start by reproducing it based on the recorded test. The information “the report doesn't work” leaves the person doing the work a lot of guessing. A description of the file, the action taken and the result received gets to the cause faster. If the error only appears sometimes, also keep the time of the test, so the corresponding record in the program can be found.
Work out what causes the problem. A timeout can come both from a mistake in your program and from a delay in an external service. Ask the person doing the work for an explanation based on checking. When the cause remains unknown, the nearest task may be exactly finding it. This helps avoid a big rebuild undertaken without knowing what needs fixing.
Run the conversation with the team so that people report problems quickly. Ask what happened and what information they had while working. If the cause was an unclear rule or different versions of the agreements, also improve the way they're passed on. Agree on one person who keeps an eye on the fix until it's checked. Just handing the task over to a developer doesn't end this work.
After the change, repeat the test that previously showed the error. Also check the parts of the program the fix may have affected. Changing how dates are saved in a report may, for example, change the order of documents in the history. This kind of check helps catch a situation in which fixing one feature breaks another. Match the scope of the tests to the change. A small text fix and a change to access rules need a different scope of checking.
Keep the earlier result, label the new version and attach the result of the repeated test to the related work. If you're updating the approved proof of a completed Goal, reopen it the way Vairo works. A goal “fix report creation” ends once correct behaviour is shown. When you haven't found a defect, this sub-point doesn't require inventing extra work.
saas/saas-check.guide_sources.0: Google SRE, Testing for Reliability describes checking a connected system and choosing tests. Stripe, Webhooks explains verifying messages and handling retries and the order of events. OWASP, Input Validation Cheat Sheet supports choosing tests with invalid data. Recording results in Goals follows from the Vairo program.
saas/saas-check.guide_sources.1: AWS, Load test your workload describes choosing the load, conditions and measurements. Google SRE, Reliable Product Launches at Scale takes usage limits into account when preparing a service. The cost example is a supporting calculation for the Vairo program.
saas/saas-check.guide_sources.2: Google SRE, Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure describes explaining causes and the conditions that encourage reporting errors. Google SRE, Testing for Reliability explains re-checking behaviour after changes. Handling proof and reopening a Goal follow from Vairo's rules.

saas/saas-check/load.title: Check the load and the cost of use
saas/saas-check/load/open.question: Write down the conditions of use, the load test result and the cost estimate.
saas/saas-check/load/open.config.label: Open goals
saas/saas-check/fix.title: Fix the problem and check the change
saas/saas-check/fix.description: No defect means no obligation to fix anything.
saas/saas-check/fix/open.question: If something blocks use, fix it in the tracker and check the change.
saas/saas-check/fix/open.config.label: Open goals
saas/saas-keep.title: Prepare the program for maintenance and updates
saas/saas-keep.guide_body:
4.1. Launch a version that can be shared and improved
Launch the prepared version in a place the first recipients will be able to use it from. During preparations you can limit access to the team. Check the main action right there, because settings that differ from those on the creator's computer can change how the program works. If you're building on a ready-made platform, use its way of publishing and check the published version.
Separate the data used for tests from the data of future recipients. Separate the settings of test and live services in the same way, especially payments. The connection to the program should be encrypted, usually through HTTPS. Keep private keys to services in the provider's settings meant for this or another suitably secured place. A key placed in code sent to the browser can be read by the user. Add to Vairo information about where access is managed, without copying secrets.
Keep the code and information about the versions of the program's necessary components. A repository, e.g. on GitHub, stores the code and the history of its changes. But the code alone may not be enough to launch it again if the right settings or information about the libraries used are missing. With a ready-made platform, use its version history or the available export. Agree with the person doing the work on what will let you recreate your app and what limitations the chosen service has.
Run an update of the prepared version, then check the main action. If several people change the program, agree on who puts together and publishes a given version. The others should know what went into this update and which tests have to be repeated. A kept record of the change will also make it easier to go back to it when explaining a later defect.
Check how you'll find out about an error and where its record can be found. Such a record, called a log, should help identify the action and the moment of the problem. Trigger a safe test error and find it. Also make it possible to establish that a user completed the main action, e.g. created a report. This information will come in handy in the MVP Stage. Limit the recorded information to what's needed; passwords and users' private materials shouldn't end up in logs or proofs.
As proof, use the address and the version label, the record of a successful update and the existing materials needed to recreate it. Attach the result of the error check and of the main action. The person reviewing the work should know where the program runs and where to look for information when it stops working correctly.
4.2. Check recovery of operation and the necessary data
Practise a situation in which an update makes the program's main action impossible. Choose with the person doing the work a way of restoring the service. It may be going back to the previous version or applying a prepared fix. Choose the test conditions so as not to damage recipients' data. You can use a separate test version or a trial app with the chosen provider.
Ask whether the update also changes the way data is saved. An older version of the program may not understand its new form. That's why going back to earlier code doesn't always restore the whole service. The technical person should take this into account in the procedure and check it together with the data. In the proof, keep the information about which update and configuration the test was run for.
If the program stores users' materials needed for further work, check restoring them from a backup. Restore test data in a separate place and open it in the program. See whether the needed action can be done with it. A provider's message about a successful backup doesn't yet show whether the team can recover usable data from it. When the app only processes information temporarily, focus on recovering operation and the necessary settings.
Write down what point in time the recovered data comes from and how long the test took. For example, a backup made the previous evening may not contain today's work. Decide whether such a recovery range is enough for the product's first use. If not, change the way backups or recovery are done. When using a ready-made platform, check the options available in your plan and practise the relevant procedure.
Keep a short description of the steps taken and the result. You can attach the provider's instructions and add only the settings needed for your app. In the team, check that the person who's meant to respond to an outage has the access needed and understands these instructions. A test Goal can end with a negative result, but before confirming the version is ready, you need a successful recovery test.
saas/saas-keep.guide_sources.0: The Twelve-Factor App, Codebase, Dependencies and Config describe versioning, dependencies and separating configuration. OWASP, Logging Cheat Sheet explains recording events and protecting information in logs. Microsoft, Safe deployment practices describes checking the changes being introduced. The variant for a ready-made platform has been adapted to the way the product is built.
saas/saas-keep.guide_sources.1: Microsoft, Safe deployment practices describes recovering operation after an update, also with data changes. AWS, Perform periodic recovery of the data to verify backup integrity and processes explains checking restored data, the recovery time and the point you can go back to.

saas/saas-ready.title: Confirm the first version is ready
saas/saas-ready.guide_body:
5.1. Confirm the specified version is ready
Name the specific version you've prepared for first use. Attach the proofs from the earlier sub-points and check that they still apply to it. If the way reports are saved changed after a test, the earlier result may need completing. Ask the person responsible for the change to point out what needs checking again. Materials that remain valid can be reused.
Go through the remaining problems in terms of the planned use. A missing extra chart color can wait. A wrong report result or the possibility of reading someone else's data make it impossible to consider the relevant feature ready. Ask about the effect on the recipient and about the proof of correct behaviour. Just the information that the person doing the work has finished coding doesn't settle these questions.
Take into account the conditions under which the tests were run. If you checked use by a small group, the confirmation applies exactly to such a start. The prepared limits should help maintain these conditions. The team should also know how it will notice a problem and how it will restore operation. Use the results of sub-points 3.2, 4.1 and 4.2.
The person collecting the proofs relies on the assessments of the people responsible for the individual parts. For matters requiring specialist knowledge, base the decision on a proper check. If an obstacle remains, point it out on the related work and leave the readiness confirmation empty. Specific information, e.g. “the test wasn't repeated after the change to file access”, lets you set the next action right away.
When the specified version meets the conditions for first use, choose “Version ready for first use”. This entry confirms the result of the SaaS category. Closing the whole of Execution happens through the General part after the necessary categories are completed. You'll go on to make the product available to recipients and collect the results of their use in the MVP Stage, using the same tracker and the gathered materials.
saas/saas-ready.guide_sources.0: Google SRE, Reliable Product Launches at Scale describes matching the readiness assessment to the service and focusing on matters affecting its launch. The confirmation conditions, reuse of proofs and moving between stages follow from the program and the Vairo CTO guidelines.
saas/saas-ready/confirm.title: Confirm the specified version is ready
saas/saas-ready/confirm/version.question: Which version are you confirming?
saas/saas-ready/confirm/version.help: Enter the label of the version the earlier proofs refer to.
saas/saas-ready/confirm/ready.question: Is this version ready for first use?

hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.intro: From requirements and safety, through a unit, to readiness for first use.
hardware/hw-spec.title: Set the requirements of the first version
hardware/hw-spec.guide_body:
1.1. Decide what you'll check before first use
Open the product description from the previous stage. Imagine its first use: who picks it up, what they want to do and in what conditions it will work. This description should show what the design has to make possible. A holder meant for calm work at a desk may need different solutions from a holder used on a moving vehicle. Link the existing description and fill in the missing information in the same place.
Write down each important requirement so that it can be decided whether it has been met. “The holder is strong” leaves too much room for guesswork. “The holder carries 5 kg for 30 minutes without slipping” points to a result that can be checked. This is an example of how to write it down. The right load, time and test conditions must follow from your product's purpose and its safety requirements.
Next to each requirement, add how you'll check it. Sometimes measuring a dimension is enough, and sometimes you'll need a functional test or an examination by a specialist. The person preparing the design and the person doing the check should understand the expected result the same way. Clearing up differences now helps avoid making a part that will later have to be ordered again.
Take the tests into account already when planning the first units. If a test may damage a part, decide beforehand whether you need a separate sample. If several people will use the same unit, agree on the order. This way the first order will cover what you need to get answers, and preparing one test won't hold up the rest of the work.
1.2. Check what's needed for the product to be safe and compliant
Work out which requirements apply to your product and the country in which you intend to make it available. Its purpose matters too. A similar-looking object may be subject to different requirements when it's used for play, work or a medical application. Start with official information for the product group. In the European Union, the Your Europe portal can be a starting point.
The CE marking applies only to certain product groups. When it's required, you have to go through the proper conformity assessment, that is checking and documenting that the relevant requirements are met. Buying a part with CE doesn't automatically confirm the compliance of the whole product you build from it. Not being required to carry the CE marking doesn't mean the product isn't subject to safety requirements either.
If you need help, give a specialist a description of the use and the available design materials. Ask them to point out what has to be taken into account in the design and what checks will be needed before the planned use. Such a specific question gets a more useful answer than a general request to “check the product”.
In the team, decide who will collect this answer and see that the needed changes are made. This person can coordinate the work, drawing on the knowledge of the right specialist. If you work alone, you can order such a consultation externally. Assign the assessment of an issue to a person who can assess it; a free slot on its own isn't enough.
Add the findings and their source to the document from sub-point 1.1. Describe an unresolved matter specifically, e.g. “It needs confirming whether the chosen material is suitable for this use”. If the answer could force a design change, clear it up before a costly order. Completing this sub-point means the requirements have been identified; confirming that they're met happens during further work.
hardware/hw-spec.guide_sources.0: NASA, Technical Requirements Definition describes translating the way of use into verifiable requirements. NASA, Product Verification explains choosing the methods and resources needed to verify them.
hardware/hw-spec.guide_sources.1: Your Europe, CE marking explains the scope of the marking and responsibility for the whole product. NASA, Technical Planning describes matching skills and responsibility to technical work.
hardware/hw-spec/checks.title: Decide what you'll check before first use
hardware/hw-spec/checks/use.question: What is the first version for, who uses it and in what conditions?
hardware/hw-spec/checks/use.help: If you already have such a description, paste it or point to the file.
hardware/hw-spec/checks/requirements.que: A document: what the product has to do, what result is enough and how you'll check it.
hardware/hw-spec/checks/requirements.hel: For a requirement that may use up a unit, include extra units.
hardware/hw-spec/safety.title: Check what's needed for the product to be safe and compliant
hardware/hw-spec/safety/rules.question: What regulations, safeguards, tests and documents apply to this use?
hardware/hw-spec/safety/rules.help: Give the source. If you don't know something, write down what needs clarifying. This is identifying the requirements, not a certificate.
hardware/hw-try.title: Check the uncertain part before building the whole
hardware/hw-try.guide_body:
2.1. Run an earlier test if its result could change the design
Look at the design and choose the unknown that could later cost you the most work. It may be a way of joining parts whose strength you don't know yet. It may also be a material that has to keep its properties in the expected conditions. An earlier test makes sense when its result will help choose the further design. If you already have suitable results for this use, use them.
Prepare only the piece of the product that will let you answer the chosen question. Two samples may be enough to check a joint. A model showing the shape can help check the fit, but conclusions about strength require the right material and way of making it. Match the sample to what you want to find out.
A Goal of the “Test result” type could read: “Check whether the chosen joint meets the load requirement from sub-point 1.1”. Set the responsible person and the deadline for getting the answer. As the expected proof, name a record of the test with the result and a conclusion. This way, even before the work starts, it's clear what it should end with.
If several people work on it, split preparing the sample, running the test and assessing the result into tasks under this Goal. In the note, explain what has to be ready before the next task starts. With a small test done alone, you can run the whole thing in one Goal. The level of detail in the split should help get the work done.
After the test, write down what was tested, in what conditions and what happened. A negative result can complete a Goal about running a test if you've got the answer you needed. The next decision may then be to change the joint or the material. Take on the next test with a specific question that the previous result hasn't answered yet.
hardware/hw-try.guide_sources.0: TWI, What is Prototyping? describes matching the prototype to the question and checking the design in stages. Michael Seibel, The Scientific Method for Startups presents working by testing assumptions and drawing conclusions. The Goal example applies these principles in Vairo.
hardware/hw-try/probe.title: Run an earlier test if its result could change the design
hardware/hw-try/probe/open.question: A goal of the “Test result” type: version, conditions, result and decision.
hardware/hw-try/probe/open.config.label: Open goals
hardware/hw-build.title: Make or order the first version of the product
hardware/hw-build.guide_body:
3.1. Make a unit that can be checked
Link the requirements and the necessary files to a Goal of the “Build result” type, describing the unit to be made. Name the version the work concerns. Also define what will show this Goal is done. A photo can confirm the object was made, and a video or an acceptance record can also show its basic operation. You'll do the detailed check of the requirements in sub-point 4.1.
Split the build into results that can be handed to the next person. For a simple holder, one task may be preparing a drawing with the mounting dimensions. The next will be making the part from this drawing. The following task will cover assembling the holder and checking the fit. Such a split shows what's to be made and what the next person is waiting for.
A task is small enough when the person responsible understands its scope and can say when it's finished. Split it further if it hides several handovers of work or its result will be invisible for a long time. Small assembly steps can stay in the instructions with the task. A separate entry is useful when it helps assign responsibility or track an important result.
Agree on the assignment with the person doing the work, taking into account their skills and available time. The Goal owner sees that the whole unit gets made, while individual tasks can be done by different people. With an external order, a person from your team keeps track of the agreements and accepts the result. Before ordering, agree with the contractor on which files they work from and what exactly they're to deliver.
If parts are made in parallel, agree beforehand on the places where they're to connect. When one person designs the enclosure and another the part placed inside it, both need matching dimensions and mounting positions. Pass any change to these agreements on to the other person before further work.
When setting the deadline, take into account waiting for the contractor or a delivery. If the product can't be assembled without the ordered part, its date affects further work. Run the remaining tasks in parallel where they already have the necessary data. When several pieces of work are waiting for one specialist or one workstation, set an order instead of giving them all the same deadline.
3.2. Keep the information needed to make this version
Collect documentation during the build. After the unit is made, it should show how exactly this version was made. If you changed a dimension or swapped a part in the workshop, reflect that in the files. A drawing of an earlier idea isn't enough to repeat the finished design.
Keep the information that will let you choose the material again and order the right parts. The entry “small motor” may lead to buying a completely different part. The specific model designation and the number of units let you recreate the choice. Such a list of parts and materials is often called a BOM. You can keep it in an ordinary document you already use for the build.
Label the version of the files and link it to the unit. When you give a contractor a new drawing, clearly state that it replaces the previous one, and confirm whether the earlier part has already been made. It's a simple way to avoid a situation in which two people work to different dimensions. In the Goal, put a link to the right materials instead of creating more copies of them.
Before ordering, talk to the contractor about how the needed number of units will be made. Ask whether the chosen shape and material suit their production method. Sometimes a small design change simplifies assembly or avoids an expensive tool. That's the basis of design for manufacturing, abbreviated DFM. At this stage you're matching the making to the first use needed.
Check the availability of the parts further building depends on, and keep the contractor's quote. If you're building alone, use the costs and experience from the first unit. Separate the cost of one-off preparation from the cost of the next unit, if there's such a difference. When assembly requires an undescribed fix or long fitting, add this information to the design. This will let you improve the design or prepare the contractor before the next order.
hardware/hw-build.guide_sources.0: NASA, Technical Planning describes work results, their order and the resources needed. NASA, Interface Management explains coordinating parts made by different people. Atlassian, Roles and Responsibilities supports distinguishing the responsible person from the collaborators. The split of the example Goal into tasks has been adapted to Vairo.
hardware/hw-build.guide_sources.1: NASA, Configuration Management describes identifying versions and controlling documentation changes. TWI, What is Design for Manufacturing? explains how design decisions affect manufacturing and assembly.

hardware/hw-test.title: Check the product and fix the problems found
hardware/hw-test.guide_body:
4.1. Check the first version against the agreed requirements
Open the requirements from point 1 and use them as the basis for the tests. One Goal can cover the whole set of checks needed. You can carve out separate tasks when the tests are done by different people or need separate preparation. The shared result should be an answer as to which requirements the specified version meets and what still needs work.
Before a test, make sure the person running it has the right unit and the current requirements. With several units, distinguish the unit number from the design version. Two units made from the same design may have a different test history. The entry “v2, unit 3” will later let you understand which object the result refers to.
For each check, set the expected result against the one obtained. Add the conditions that could have affected it. If the test concerned the device's running time, also give the way it was used. Choose the evidence to suit the question: a photo can show a crack, but a time measurement requires a record of the result obtained. Keep the data right as you run the test.
In the team, agree on using a shared unit. The person passing it on should say what tests it has gone through and whether they noticed any damage. Match the order and the use of separate samples to the chosen test method. Entrust tests requiring suitable equipment or qualifications to a person or facility that has them.
If someone else can review the results, ask them to check that they match the requirements. When working alone, go back to the recorded criteria before you consider a test successful. A completed Goal of the “Test result” type confirms that the test was run and the answer recorded. An unmet requirement still needs a decision and appropriate action before the product is confirmed as ready.
4.2. Remove the problem and check the fix
Start by working out exactly what happened. Use the test record and check at what moment the problem appeared. A part cracking is an observation. Saying the cause was the wrong material needs checking, because the way it was made or assembled may also have mattered. If the cause remains unknown, the nearest task will be to find it.
Base the conversation with the team on what can be checked. Ask which drawing was used and what information was available during the work. Thank them for reporting the error quickly. A person who fears the team's reaction may put off passing on a problem, and meanwhile the others will be working on a wrong assumption. After finding the cause, agree on a specific change. If an old drawing caused the mistake, also improve the way current files are passed on.
Describe in the related Goal what you're changing and what result is to confirm the fix works. A task of changing the drawing may be done earlier, but a Goal about removing the defect still needs the new design checked. Assign these activities according to the skills of the people doing them. The person coordinating the fix makes sure the work reaches this final check.
When possible, check the effect of one change at a time. If you change several things at once, keep information about all the changes, so the result obtained can be explained later. Label the new version and keep access to the earlier results.
Also assess what else the fix affected. A thicker part may carry the load better but no longer fit in the mounting place. Repeat the checks on the changed part and on the parts of the product the change affects. Agree on the scope of the repeat tests with a person who can assess these dependencies. Attach the result of the fix to the existing work in Vairo.
hardware/hw-test.guide_sources.0: NASA, Product Verification describes checking requirements and preparing tests. NASA, Configuration Management explains identifying the version tested. The way of recording the result in a Goal follows from Vairo's rules.
hardware/hw-test.guide_sources.1: John Lunney and Sue Lueder, Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure describes analyzing causes and creating conditions for reporting problems; these team working principles are applied here to building hardware. NASA, Configuration Management describes assessing the impact of changes and checking them.

hardware/hw-test/trial/open.question: The proof contains the results of the checks required for first use.
hardware/hw-test/trial/open.config.label: Open goals
hardware/hw-test/fix.title: Remove the problem and check the fix

hardware/hw-ready.title: Prepare the product for first use
hardware/hw-ready.guide_body:
5.1. Prepare the needed unit and the materials for use
Prepare the number of units that follows from the first planned use. It may be one installation or several units handed to recipients. Use the documentation of the checked version. With further units, pay attention to whether the contractor kept to the agreed material and way of making it. A substitute proposed during assembly may require the design to be checked again.
Separate the results concerning the design from the inspection of the prepared unit. Checking the design helps establish whether it meets the requirements. Accepting a specific unit lets you catch a defect in how it was made, e.g. a missing part or wrong assembly. The scope of such an inspection should match your product and the requirements from point 1. Keep the result with the unit it concerns.
For first use, choose a unit in suitable condition. Check its test history, especially when the tests may have weakened or damaged it. If different people do the assembly and the inspection, give them the same current materials. When working alone, you can do both, using the recorded requirements and a specialist's help where needed.
Prepare instructions based on what the user will be doing. Explain how to prepare the product and how to use it correctly. Describe the limitations and warnings that follow from its design. If the way of using it is hard to show in words, add a photo or a drawing. If the product needs installing, pass the relevant information to the person who will install it too.
Attach the documents and markings needed for this product and the planned use, according to the findings from sub-point 1.2. The materials should match the prepared version. Use the existing results and files. If the product will be transported, also make sure it's protected for the journey, so it arrives in a condition that allows the intended use.
5.2. Confirm the specified version is ready
State exactly which version is ready for the agreed use. Attach its check results and the materials prepared in sub-point 5.1. A person reviewing this record should be able to link the finished unit to the documentation and understand on what basis you considered it ready.
Go back to the requirements from point 1. Check that you have an answer for each of them and whether a problem remains that prevents the intended use. In teamwork, the person collecting the results relies on the assessments of the people responsible for the individual areas. In matters requiring specialist knowledge, base the decision on a proper assessment or test.
If someone raises a doubt, explain which requirement it concerns and what's missing to settle it. For example, the information “the test result after the material change is missing” points to specific further work. As long as the requirements for the planned use remain unmet, leave the confirmation empty and record the obstacle on the relevant work.
Ideas for extra features can stay in the notes for later. You assess readiness against the agreed use and its requirements. If you want to change the use itself, first check what requirements and tests follow from that change. Just rewriting the description doesn't solve a design problem.
When you have the needed confirmations and there are no obstacles blocking the specified use, mark the version as ready. Vairo collects the record of this decision and the related proofs. The technical assessment and responsibility for approving the product for use remain with the appropriate people. Keep the link to this version, so you know later which product went into first use and what the feedback received refers to.
hardware/hw-ready.guide_sources.0: NASA, Product Transition describes handing over a checked product with its documentation and preparing for its use. Your Europe, CE marking explains the obligations concerning proper documentation and marking of products covered by CE.
hardware/hw-ready.guide_sources.1: NASA, Product Transition describes handing over a product based on its condition and documentation. NASA, Product Verification explains checking that requirements are met. The way of confirming readiness and attaching proofs follows from how Vairo works.

hardware/hw-ready/pack/control.help: You can point to materials already used in the build and the test, if they concern this version.

b2b.title: B2B
b2b.intro: Prepare the handover to the company and rehearse the path from the start to the result received.
b2b/b2b-hand.title: Prepare the solution for use in a company
b2b/b2b-hand.guide_body:
1.1. Prepare the first handover to the company
Open the findings from Preparation and choose the first use you're preparing the product for. Draw on the recorded roles and the requirements for starting work. On this basis, prepare what you'll actually hand over to the company. A short message with the program's address and the way of passing data may be enough. For a device, instructions may be needed for the person installing it at the workplace.
In this message, separate your team's actions from the customer's. If the company is to provide a file, show how to prepare it and where to send it. If someone has to prepare a workstation, give them the necessary information before delivery. Finished instructions should help do the action without guessing or searching old messages for answers.
Pay attention to handing over the result. For example, an employee may collect data and prepare a summary that a manager later receives. Check in what form the manager needs this summary. Prepare the necessary document or way of sharing it, using the features already being built in SaaS or the Hardware materials. In a small company, one person may do these tasks.
If the company earlier named a document or approval needed to start, prepare your part. Point out what still requires the customer's decision. Your own description doesn't replace the company's approval. In an internal test such a handover can be simulated, but checking the conditions of a specific customer remains necessary before starting cooperation.
In the Goal, name one result, e.g. “A prepared handover of the summary from the employee to the manager”. The owner makes sure the materials fit the same version of the product. Extra tasks are useful when the instructions and the product part are prepared by different people. The proof is the finished materials that can be used in the first cooperation.
b2b/b2b-hand.guide_sources.0: GOV.UK, Solve a whole problem for users (fitting the whole flow to the recipient's work); Paul Graham, Do Things that Don’t Scale (personal help for the first companies and a simple way to start).
b2b/b2b-hand/pack.title: Prepare the first handover to the company
b2b/b2b-hand/pack/open.question: A goal with finished materials for starting and handing over the result.
b2b/b2b-hand/pack/open.config.label: Open goals
b2b/b2b-try.title: Check the solution's use in the company's work
b2b/b2b-try.guide_body:
2.1. Rehearse the flow from the start to receiving the result
Use one specific example from earlier conversations. For a reporting tool, it may be an employee preparing a weekly summary and a manager receiving it. For a service, do a trial scope of work and prepare the result the company would receive. A working version is required; a description of the future flow alone doesn't show whether it can be gone through.
Split the test by who does the next thing. One person can play several roles if you work alone. Stop at each handover and check whether the next recipient has the material they need and understands what to do with it. A common problem is a result that was created but went to the wrong person or isn't fit for further use.
You can invite a representative of the company. Give them a task that matches their work and watch where they need an explanation. When the customer's participation isn't possible right now, run an internal test and describe it as such. Such a record shows a check of the prepared flow. You'll confirm the fit to the conditions of a specific company during the cooperation.
Take into account the help you intend to provide at the start. If you personally set up the solution for each company, also do this part of the test. Keep useful settings or instructions. If the work passes between your collaborators, agree on who receives a given piece and where they'll find the result. One person is responsible for seeing the whole Goal through.
In the proof, write down the example, the version and the result. The sentence “The employee prepared the summary, but the manager couldn't open the file” points to a specific fix. After the change, redo the necessary part. A negative result lets you complete a Goal about running the test; readiness in 2.2 requires removing the obstacles in the agreed flow.
2.2. Confirm readiness for first use in a company
Go through the finished materials and the test result for the specified version. Check whether the company can make the necessary preparations, whether the employee will get the result and whether it will go on to where it's needed. Use the existing files. This confirmation doesn't require writing another summary of the whole project.
Agree with the person running the test whether obstacles preventing such use remain. Missing starter materials or an undone handover of the result need finishing. An idea for serving another department can wait if the current version is meant to serve one team. Assess the scope according to the earlier findings.
If the product version or the way of handover changed after the test, work out what needs checking again. Attach the new result to the same work and keep the earlier record. For matters requiring a technical assessment, use the right person to do it. The requirements specific to the product still apply in the other chosen categories.
The confirmation concerns readiness for the first agreed use. It doesn't require a signed contract, a paying customer or proof of sales growth. An internal test stays marked as internal. In the MVP Stage you'll be able to check how the solution works in further conditions with recipients and what needs improving.
b2b/b2b-try.guide_sources.0: GOV.UK, Using moderated usability testing (a test on a specific task and observing the participant's difficulties); GOV.UK, Provide a joined up experience across all channels (checking the handover of work between people and contact channels).
b2b/b2b-try.guide_sources.1: GOV.UK, How the beta phase works (gradually making the prepared service available and further improvements).

b2c.title: B2C
b2c.intro: Prepare the offer for the consumer and rehearse the path from receiving the product to reporting a problem.
b2c/b2c-offer.title: Prepare the offer for the consumer
b2c/b2c-offer.guide_body:
1.1. Put the necessary information where the choice is made
Prepare the material you'll use for the first order or sign-up. Start with what the customer will get and when they'll be able to use it. Describe the current version according to its capabilities. If the product will be ready later, say so clearly. A place already chosen for contact or sales is enough, e.g. an offer on an existing platform or a message to the customer.
Use the earlier price and add the necessary terms. For a specific order, the customer should know how much they'll pay in total, including any mandatory delivery costs. If the price can't reasonably be calculated in advance, check the relevant information obligations and give the way it's calculated. With a recurring fee, show the billing period, the terms for ending it and any minimum commitment period.
Match the information to the way the contract is concluded. Selling online may require providing different information than selling in person. Use your country's consumer authority pages; for Poland, the UOKiK pages listed below. Fill in the correct seller details, contact and complaint rules. Also check the right of withdrawal, that is the possibility of backing out of the contract in certain situations. The scope of this right and its exceptions depend on the offer. Avoid copying the terms of a shop selling a completely different product.
With an electronic order requiring payment, also check that the customer clearly sees they're placing an order with an obligation to pay. The necessary information has to appear at the right moment. A document stored on your side doesn't mean the customer received it. A ready-made sales platform may provide some of the needed features; check your configuration and the content you entered.
Assign the Goal to the person who will put together the finished offer. One person can prepare the text and another place it with the order. Pass legal matters needing clarification to the right specialist. As proof, keep the content used and where it's placed. This way a later change to the page won't erase the information about what was checked.
b2c/b2c-offer.guide_sources.0: UOKiK, Right to information (clear information matched to the way the contract is concluded); UOKiK, Off-premises and distance selling (price, offer terms and information in distance selling); UOKiK, Withdrawal from a contract (withdrawal and situations requiring the right rules to be checked).
b2c/b2c-offer/place.title: Put the necessary information where the choice is made
b2c/b2c-offer/place/open.question: A goal with the finished offer where the choice is made.
b2c/b2c-offer/place/open.config.label: Open goals
b2c/b2c-path.title: Check the customer's whole path
b2c/b2c-path.guide_body:
2.1. Rehearse receiving the product and reporting a problem
Choose one offer you want to make available at the start. Go through it the way a new customer will: from reading the description to getting the promised result. For a digital file, check receiving and opening it. For a physical product, prepare a test order and check that the right unit is handed over. For a service, do a test within the promised scope.
Also watch the work on your side. If the order comes to one person and another hands over the product, check that the second one gets the necessary information. With a small number of customers, you can do part of the handling by hand. Rehearse the chosen way, including the work the customer doesn't see.
With a payment gateway, use the test mode described by the provider. For Stripe, this is the test environment and test payment details. If a suitable check was done in SaaS, attach that result and here fill in only the missing parts of the consumer's path. Pay attention to whether the customer gets the right confirmation and whether the order reaches handling.
Then send a sample report through the contact given. Check who receives it and how they get to a reply or the needed action. A complaint concerns a problem with the purchased service; withdrawing from a contract may have a different basis and course. For the test, choose a situation that concerns your product and apply the right rules. An ordinary contact inbox may be enough for first handling if someone checks it and can deal with the matter.
You can ask a person outside the team to go through the prepared path. Watch where they need additional explanation. With a test done on your own, write down who did it; don't conclude from it that every person will understand the offer. In one Goal, keep the result of receiving the product, the report test and the problems found. A negative result is a completed check, but requires a suitable fix before 2.2.
2.2. Confirm readiness to serve the first customer
Compare the offer with the test result. A promise to deliver a file right after ordering should match what the customer will receive. If you need human help and more time, the offer should take that into account. Check the price, the scope of the first version and the way of starting to use it in the same way.
Go through the problems found. A wrong amount at checkout, a missing promised material or a non-working contact need fixing before confirmation. An extra product variant or a referral program can stay for later. You're assessing the readiness of the chosen start, so use the agreed scope.
After the fix, repeat the part the change concerned and attach the result to the same work. If the offer was changed after the test, check that the result still matches its content. Assigning one person to collect the materials helps catch a mismatch between what the description promises and what the person doing the work prepared.
Confirm readiness when you have the necessary proofs and the obstacles are resolved. This record doesn't confirm demand or the effectiveness of advertising. In the MVP Stage you'll make the first version available to recipients and check how they use it. The materials and Goals will stay in the same place, so feedback after launch can be linked to a specific version.
